pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: Walk me through the standard fan-out shape: a loop that starts one goroutine per item and returns only when all are done. What does each WaitGroup call do, and where exactly does each one live?
expected_points: go f() starts f in a new goroutine and returns immediately — no result, no join handle; arguments are evaluated at the go statement
Add increments the counter before each go; Done — deferred, inside the goroutine — decrements; Wait blocks until the counter is zero
the function returns only after Wait, and deferring Done means an early return or panic in the task still counts down

questions.prompt: Why can a Go program run hundreds of thousands of goroutines when the same machine struggles with a few thousand OS threads — and what happens to all of them the moment main returns?
expected_points: goroutines start with a tiny (~2KB) growable stack; OS threads reserve megabytes up front
the Go runtime schedules goroutines in user space onto a small pool of OS threads (GOMAXPROCS), so switching avoids kernel context-switch cost
when main returns the process exits immediately: every other goroutine is killed mid-flight, no message, no deferred calls run — nothing waits unless you make it wait

questions.prompt: In the exercise you wrote Total with one shared counter first and ran go test -race. What is a data race, what did the report show you, and how did you fix the code?
expected_points: a data race: two goroutines access the same memory concurrently, at least one a write, with nothing ordering them — total++ is read/modify/write, not one step, and racy programs have undefined behavior
the report shows the shared address and two stack traces (the conflicting access and the previous one), each with the goroutine and where it was created
the fix is ownership: each worker sums into its own cell (distinct slice elements are distinct memory) and the cells are combined only after Wait

questions.prompt: Why must wg.Add(1) happen before the go statement rather than as the first line inside the goroutine? Describe the interleaving that breaks.
expected_points: the scheduler makes no promise about when a new goroutine first runs; it may not have executed Add when Wait checks the counter
so Wait can observe zero, return early, and the function finishes while the work is still running or has not started
Add must run in the launching goroutine, sequenced before go and hence before Wait; Add(len) up front is equally correct

questions.prompt: A worker goroutine does `if err != nil { return }` above its wg.Done() line. What is a goroutine leak, who leaks in this code, and what habit makes the bug impossible?
expected_points: a leak is a goroutine that can never proceed or terminate; Go cannot kill it from outside, so its stack and everything it references stay live for the life of the process
the leak is the waiter: the counter never reaches zero, so whoever called Wait blocks forever — the failed worker itself exited cleanly
defer wg.Done() as the goroutine's first statement, so every exit path counts down

questions.prompt: In Map, goroutines write into out[i] and the caller reads the whole slice after Wait — no locks anywhere. Why is that not a data race?
expected_points: each goroutine writes a distinct element — distinct memory locations — so the writers never conflict with each other
WaitGroup supplies the ordering: each write happens before its Done, and every Done happens before Wait returns, so the caller's reads are ordered after all writes
the same reads performed before Wait would be a race — the synchronization, not the slice, makes it safe

questions.prompt: Your test suite has been -race clean for a month. A colleague says that proves the code is race-free. Are they right?
expected_points: no — the detector is dynamic: it only sees conflicting accesses that actually execute in that run, with that schedule and those inputs
a clean run raises confidence but says nothing about untaken paths; a reported race, by contrast, is always a real bug
so keep tests running under -race routinely — the 2-20x time/memory cost is affordable in tests
